case_data.title: Designing Responsible AI Systems with Indigenous Communities: A Participatory Approach for the Himba and San Communities in Namibia
case_data.provide-a-brief-description-of-the-proje:
**Led by academic researchers in collaboration with local elders, this 2024 initiative engaged at least 30 members of Namibia's Ovahimba and San communities through co-creation workshops and prototyping. By centering local cultural values and Indigenous Knowledge Systems, the project aimed to establish trustworthy, context-specific AI tools while developing reusable participatory methodologies.**

This research investigates participatory and responsible Artificial Intelligence (RAI) practices within three interconnected AI-driven projects focused on Namibia’s Indigenous communities, specifically the Ovahimba and San. Three AI-driven projects; Himbaverse, Smart Hydroponics, and Resilience App, were explored and implemented through a co-design process. 

The projects aim to promote responsible AI development that enhance trust and aligns with local community aspirations, needs and goals of sustainability and integration of Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) with advanced technology to empower local cultures. The research is based on participatory design processes and technology prototyping with Ovahimba and San communities in Namibia. It shows that transparency and active participation empower communities to contribute to development of evolving knowledge bases and system capabilities of RAI. 

Preliminary findings reveal that responsible AI design must be deeply contextual and shaped by local cultural values, knowledge systems, and community-defined objectives. The study contributes to the growing discourse on participatory AI development, demonstrating how culturally responsive and responsible AI systems can empower Indigenous communities and promote equitable technological integration.
case_data.headline-findings:
Across the three cases, several transferable practices emerged: (1) treating AI systems as evolving collaborators rather than fixed tools; (2) grounding transparency in culturally meaningful metaphors; (3) prioritising participatory processual representations over static outputs; and (4) embedding learning and capacity-building as core design outcomes. These practices provide actionable guidance for researchers and practitioners seeking to operationalise responsible and participatory AI in other Indigenous contexts.
The paper has demonstrated how RAI can be enacted through participatory, community-centred design with Indigenous communities in Namibia. By grounding AI development in local knowledge systems, cultural values, and long-term relationships, the three cases illustrate how global ethical principles can be translated into situated practices and lifeworlds. Rather than offering a universal framework, this work contributes empirical insights, design practices, and relational methods that support culturally grounded, ethical, and resilient AI futures.
case_data.additional-acknowledgements: NAFTALI NDEAPO INDONGO, RACHEL CHARLOTTE SMITH, SHORTY KANDJENGO, UARIAIKE MBINGE, HEIKE WINSCHIERS-THEOPHILUS
case_data.inclusion-efforts: In each community, the processes were led by a community elder, who recruited m/f members of the youth and community to join on a voluntary basis. Approximately 10-20 participants actively participated in each session. The first field trips explored aspects of trust, cultural validity and relatability in the two sites, as well as providing understandings of what responsible AI, algorithms, and automated systems might mean in each of these contexts. Based on ongoing research collaboration and ethical protocols between NUST and the two sites, including set compensations for translation, coordination, and engagement, were adhered to.
